Goodness, the woman could talk. It would have been improper for me to point out how late it was, or how tired and sleepy I felt. I wished I'd gone to bed while I still had the chance. Now there was nothing for it but to endure. Her bright chatter continued through the otherwise deep, eerie silence of the sleeping castle, until at last a distant noise came from somewhere far beneath us, like a muffled scream. There was such agony in it that my skin crawled. The queen paused, her eyes bright with pleasure, and inclined her elegant head like a bird listening. Once again the sound pierced its way up through the silence.

“What is that?” I asked.

“A truly stubborn soul, with remarkable endurance. It's been hours now.”

“Enduring what?”

“The rack. Come—you'll see something entertaining. If he won't reveal his secret now, you'll see him torn apart.”

What a smooth, silky devil she was, so calm and untroubled, while the tendons down my legs ached in sympathy with the man's suffering. Armored guards carrying blazing torches led us through echoing passageways and down damp, dripping stone stairs that smelled of mold and centuries of captive darkness. It was a long, chilling, uncanny journey, and the witch's conversation made it neither shorter nor more cheerful. She was describing the sufferer and his offense. An unnamed informer had accused him of killing a stag in the royal hunting grounds. I said:

“Anonymous evidence isn't exactly fair, Your Highness. It would be more just to let the accused face his accuser.”

“I hadn't considered that; it scarcely matters. But even if I wanted to, I couldn't. His accuser arrived at night in a mask, told the forester, and immediately left again. So the forester doesn't know who he is.”

“Then this unknown man is the only person who witnessed the stag being killed?”

“Why, _nobody_ actually _saw_ it killed. But the stranger saw this defiant wretch near the place where the stag was lying, and came to report him to the forester out of devoted loyalty.”

“So the stranger was near the dead stag himself? Isn't it possible that he was the one who killed it? That devoted loyalty—behind a mask—seems a little suspicious. But why do you want the prisoner tortured, Your Highness? What good will it do?”

“He won't confess otherwise, and then his soul would be lost. The law demands his life for his crime—and I will certainly make sure he pays it! But my own soul would be in danger if I let him die without confession and absolution.

At Warwick Castle I first encountered the singular stranger of whom I am about to speak. Three qualities drew me to him: his frank simplicity, his extraordinary knowledge of ancient armor, and the repose one found in his society—for he supplied all the conversation. As retiring people often do, we found ourselves together at the rear of the flock being conducted through the place, and he promptly began saying things that caught my interest. His speech flowed on, gentle, agreeable, unbroken, and he appeared to slip almost unnoticeably from our world and age into a distant time and an old country long forgotten. Little by little he cast such enchantment over me that I seemed to walk among the ghosts and shades, the dust and mildew of dim antiquity, conversing with a surviving fragment of it! Of Sir Bedivere, Sir Bors de Ganis, Sir Launcelot of the Lake, Sir Galahad, and the other mighty names of the Round Table, he spoke precisely as I should of intimate friends or enemies or neighbors I knew best—and as he proceeded, how ancient he began to seem, how immeasurably old, faded, withered, dusty, and musty! At length he faced me and remarked, as casually as one might mention the weather or another everyday subject—

“You have heard of the transmigration of souls; what do you know of the transposition of ages—and bodies?”

I answered that I knew nothing of it. He took so little interest—much as people do in weather talk—that he failed to observe whether I answered at all. A brief silence followed, broken almost at once by the monotonous tones of the paid guide:

“An ancient hauberk, sixth century, the period of King Arthur and the Round Table; reputed to have been worn by Sir Sagramor le Desirous. Note the circular hole in the chain-mail over the left breast. Unexplained; thought to have been made by a bullet after firearms were invented—possibly an act of spite by Cromwell's men.”

My companion smiled—not with any smile of today, but with one that surely had ceased to be common centuries upon centuries before—and murmured, seemingly to himself:

“Know ye well, _I beheld it done_.” After a little silence he added, “It was I that did it.”

Before I could recover from the shock that declaration gave me, he had disappeared.

Throughout that evening I remained beside my fire at the Warwick Arms, absorbed in dreams of former days, with rain striking the windows and wind bellowing round the eaves and corners. Now and then I opened old Sir Thomas Malory's delightful book, took nourishment from its sumptuous banquet of marvels and adventures, inhaled the perfume of its antiquated names, and returned to dreaming.

What kind of life could they have while Fate still left this dreadful future undecided? The wedding had to be delayed, whatever the cost. He was absolutely certain of that. He loved the girl deeply; when they sat together, even the touch of her fingers sent a delicious thrill through every nerve. Still, he understood clearly what his duty was. He knew he had no right to marry before he had committed the murder. Once it was done, he could stand beside Sybil Merton at the altar and place his life in her hands without fearing that he was doing wrong. Once it was done, he could hold her close, certain that she would never have to blush on his account or lower her head in shame. But the deed had to come first, and the sooner it happened, the better for them both.

Many men in his place would have chosen the easy pleasures of romance over the difficult climb of duty. Lord Arthur, however, had too strong a conscience to put pleasure ahead of principle. His love involved more than passion; Sybil represented everything good and noble to him. For a moment he felt a natural disgust at what was required of him, but that soon faded. His heart assured him that this was a sacrifice, not a sin, while his reason told him no other choice existed. He must decide whether to live for himself or for others. However dreadful his task, he knew he could not allow selfishness to defeat love. Sooner or later, all of us must make that same decision; all of us face the same question. For Lord Arthur it arrived early, before middle age could spoil his character with its cold, calculating distrust, or the shallow, fashionable selfishness of the times could eat away his heart. He therefore felt no hesitation about fulfilling his duty. Luckily for him, he was neither a mere dreamer nor someone who dabbled idly in things. If he had been, he would have hesitated like Hamlet and let indecision undermine his purpose. Instead, he was a thoroughly practical man. To him, life meant acting rather than thinking. He possessed that rarest of qualities: common sense.

By now the wild, confused feelings of the night before had vanished completely. He looked back almost with embarrassment at his frantic wandering through the streets and the fierce emotional pain he had suffered. The very depth and sincerity of that suffering now made it seem unreal. How, he wondered, could he have been foolish enough to rage and complain about something that could not be avoided?
